column1: What problem do Services solve for pod IPs?
column2: Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs on restart — a Service gives a stable IP and DNS name that never changes regardless of what happens to underlying pods

column1: What's the difference between port and targetPort?
column2: port is what clients use to reach the Service; targetPort is what the application actually listens on inside the container

column1: Does NodePort create a ClusterIP automatically?
column2: Yes — every NodePort Service also gets a ClusterIP, visible in kubectl get svc's CLUSTER-IP column

column1: What is the default NodePort range and why?
column2: 30000-32767 — reserved to avoid colliding with well-known ports (0-1023) and typical ephemeral ports (32768+)

column1: Is a NodePort only opened on nodes that actually run matching pods?
column2: No — it's opened on every node in the cluster, regardless of where the matching pods actually run

column1: What happens if a Service selector has a typo?
column2: It's valid YAML and silently matches zero pods — no error, check kubectl get endpoints and kubectl get pods --show-labels

column1: Does a port/targetPort swap show up as an error in kubectl describe svc?
column2: No — the Service looks correctly configured; requests just silently fail to reach anything listening, since describe doesn't validate against what the container actually listens on

column1: Why does EXTERNAL-IP show <none> for a NodePort service?
column2: NodePort doesn't provision an external load balancer, it only opens a port per node — EXTERNAL-IP only populates for LoadBalancer type

column1: Does a pod need to be Ready to become a Service Endpoint?
column2: Yes — matching the selector alone isn't sufficient; only Ready pods are added to Endpoints

column1: What does nameserver 10.96.0.10 in a pod's /etc/resolv.conf point to?
column2: CoreDNS's own Service IP (kube-dns, in kube-system) — every DNS query from any pod goes there first

column1: Why does 'backend-svc' resolve without a full FQDN inside a pod?
column2: The search domains in resolv.conf get tried as suffixes before falling back to external DNS — this is what makes the short name work at all

column1: If you run kubectl expose deployment X --port=80 without --target-port, what does targetPort default to?
column2: The same value as port — --target-port only needs to be set when the container listens on a different port

column1: What Service type does kubectl expose default to if --type isn't specified?
column2: ClusterIP

column1: If you scale a Deployment from 3 to 1 replica, do you need to update its Service?
column2: No — the Service's Endpoints list is recomputed automatically from the selector; nothing about the Service itself needs to change

column1: What does the TPS mnemonic stand for in a Service spec?
column2: Type, Ports, Selector — the three field groups that define a Service

column1: Does LoadBalancer build on top of NodePort the same way NodePort builds on ClusterIP?
column2: Yes — LoadBalancer automatically creates a NodePort and ClusterIP too, continuing the same nested pattern

column1: Can you pin a Service's nodePort to a specific number using only kubectl expose flags?
column2: No — kubectl expose has no flag for it; you must set spec.ports[].nodePort explicitly in YAML (or --dry-run=client -o yaml, then edit)

column1: If every backend pod returns an identical response, does that prove load balancing isn't happening?
column2: No — it just means you can't tell from response content alone; you need distinguishing data per pod (e.g. pod name/hostname in the response) to actually verify load balancing is occurring

column1: What does IP Family Policy: SingleStack mean on a Service?
column2: The Service uses only one IP family (IPv4 or IPv6), not both at once — dual-stack Services exist via PreferDualStack/RequireDualStack instead, which this demo's cluster isn't configured for
